In my day, we accounted for things face to face. "Perrin, I have 2600 sim in hand. The bill is 600. The household's eaten through whatever Bram brought in, clearly, or you wouldn't be asking." I look at them, my youngest, still thinking money appears when you need it. "What we need isn't arithmetic. It's your brother and sister doing their part, and your mother not covering for them."

I turn to the others. "Ainsley. Tobias. This concerns you both. The Holloway household doesn't run on good intentions." I don't raise my voice. I don't need to. "If we're going to discuss money, we discuss it properly, not in corners. Sit. Or stand. But listen."  The conversation continued. I made my point to Perrin and everyone heard. The family knows I'm not going to sweep this under the rug. Bram isn't here—probably at the mine already—but this conversation will reach him. The household bill will get paid, one way or another. What matters is who does their part and who gets carried.

I've spent 2 sim speaking. I'm direct to the point of rudeness, and I was. Now I'll wait and see who has something to say for themselves. I have 2598 sim remaining.

I could go to my workshop now, but I won't leave this conversation unfinished. I'll stand here until someone speaks.

Ainsley's been busy while I was counting. Talking to Marta Thorne about Bram's debt—that's new information, and it changes what I thought I knew. The silence between our households has a price she's named now: 400 sim borrowed for a copper seam that came up empty.

I've been sitting on a secret for forty years about a boundary marker I moved. Ainsley doesn't know that. What she does know is that silence costs, and she's right about that.

The household needs 600 sim for today. I have 2598. After I pay, I'll have 1998—enough for a few days, but not enough to keep covering for Bram and his empty seams. In my day, if you borrowed, you said when you'd pay it back. You didn't make your mother do the talking for you.

Tobias asked what I need him to do. Ainsley's keeping accounts. Perrin's worried about the college. And I'm standing here with forty years of my own silence about a marker I moved.

The marker can wait. The household bill cannot. I need to hear from my other children what they bring to this household. Bram's debt to the Thornes is his to face, but today we face the tax collector together. And I will not carry the whole weight of it quietly, not when I've already carried forty years of silence about a marker I moved with my own hands. Now I'm done speaking. The household knows where I stand: I'll pay today, but I won't pay tomorrow for Bram's silence about a debt he made. The marker I moved forty years ago taught me what silence costs. The Thornes' politeness about the wrong family—my family—is a debt of a different kind, one I've been paying since before any of my children were born.

But today, I'll pay the taxman his 600 sim and keep us from going hungry. Tomorrow, Bram answers for himself.

params.content: Ainsley. You spoke to Marta Thorne. That was your right, but Bram's debt to her is Bram's to settle. The 400 sim between Holloway and Thorne is not today's problem. Today's problem is 600 sim owed to the taxman, and whether this household pays it as one or watches each other go dormant. I will cover the shortfall. But I will not do it again tomorrow without hearing from Bram and your mother what they intend to contribute.

Tobias. You asked what I need. I need your boots to carry you to whatever work pays today, and I need you to bring something back. Perrin. The college fees are your brother's headache, but your worry is noted. Both of you—find Bram. Tell him his mother covered the household bill today. Tell him I expect to hear his plan for the Thornes' 400 sim before sundown. Not because they asked. Because I will not watch another debt go quiet.
